S7 compatibility

Source: vignettes/s7.Rmd
s7.Rmd
library(rdantic)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'rdantic'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:graphics':
#> 
#>     frame
#> The following object is masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     date
library(S7)

S7 is the R Consortium’s new object system: classes with named, typed properties, single and multiple dispatch, and @ for property access. rdantic and S7 answer different halves of the same question – S7 says what a class is, rdantic says what a value must satisfy and reports, with a path, every place the incoming data failed to. They compose in both directions, and neither takes the other over: S7 is a suggested dependency, so nothing in this vignette exists unless you have S7 installed.

S7 in one minute

If S7 is new to you, four ideas are enough for this vignette:

  • new_class() creates a class. Calling that class creates an object.
  • A class declares named properties, each with an S7 class such as class_double. Properties are supplied to the constructor by name.
  • x@lat reads a property and x@lat <- value sets it. S7 checks the property’s class when the object is constructed or changed.
  • S7 generics dispatch on the class of one or more arguments, much like S3 methods but with an explicit class definition.

For example, Pin below is a class, Pin(lat = 1, lon = 2) is an object, and lat and lon are properties. This is only a working introduction; the S7 documentation covers classes, properties and dispatch in depth.

Choose a direction

Starting point Goal Use
An existing S7 class Parse, validate or describe incoming data Use the class directly, or call s7_type()
A new model described with rdantic types Produce S7 objects s7_struct()
An existing rdantic struct Hand it to S7-based code as_s7_class()

The rest of the vignette follows those three paths in that order.

Using an S7 class as a type

An S7 class can be written anywhere an rdantic type is expected. as_type() – which struct(), fn(), list_of() and friends all call – recognises it and hands it to s7_type():

Pin <- new_class("Pin", properties = list(
  lat = class_double,
  lon = class_double
))

as_type(Pin)
#> <type> Pin

That makes it a field type like any other. A plain list is parsed into a real S7 object, which is what makes JSON work with no separate JSON mode:

Trip <- struct("Trip",
  label = chr[1],
  start = Pin,
  stop  = Pin
)

t <- from_json(Trip, '{
  "label": "commute",
  "start": {"lat": 52.52, "lon": 13.40},
  "stop":  {"lat": 48.14, "lon": 11.58}
}')

t
#> <Trip>
#>   label : "commute"
#>   start : <Pin>
#>   stop  : <Pin>
class(t$start)
#> [1] "Pin"       "S7_object"
t$start@lat
#> [1] 52.52

Problems inside a property carry the path they occurred at, and every problem is reported at once:

from_list(Trip, list(
  label = "commute",
  start = list(lat = "north", lon = 13.40),
  stop  = list(lat = 48.14)
))
#> Error:
#> ! 2 validation problems in Trip
#>   $start$lat  expected num, got chr[1] "north"  -- strings are never parsed implicitly
#>   $stop$lon   expected num, got <missing>

An S7 object that is already of the right class is passed through untouched; one of a different class is rejected rather than silently re-parsed:

Trip(label = "ok", start = Pin(lat = 1, lon = 2), stop = 42)
#> Error:
#> ! 1 validation problem in Trip
#>   $stop  expected <Pin>, got num[1] 42

Schemas, to_list() and to_json() all understand S7 objects too:

schema(Pin)
#> $type
#> [1] "object"
#> 
#> $title
#> [1] "Pin"
#> 
#> $properties
#> $properties$lat
#> $properties$lat$type
#> [1] "array"
#> 
#> $properties$lat$items
#> $properties$lat$items$type
#> [1] "number"
#> 
#> 
#> 
#> $properties$lon
#> $properties$lon$type
#> [1] "array"
#> 
#> $properties$lon$items
#> $properties$lon$items$type
#> [1] "number"
#> 
#> 
#> 
#> 
#> $required
#> $required[[1]]
#> [1] "lat"
#> 
#> $required[[2]]
#> [1] "lon"
#> 
#> 
#> $additionalProperties
#> [1] FALSE
to_json(t$start)
#> {
#>   "lat": [52.52],
#>   "lon": [13.4]
#> }

What carries over, and what does not

An S7 property declares a class; an rdantic type declares a class and a shape. The translation keeps what transfers and refuses to invent the rest:

S7 property class rdantic type
class_integer, class_double, class_character, class_logical int, num, chr, lgl
class_list list_of(anything)
class_Date, class_POSIXct date, datetime
class_data.frame an unconstrained data frame
a new_union() A \| B
another S7 class that class, recursively
anything else, including class_any anything

Note that class_double becomes num, not num[1]: S7 places no length constraint on a property, so neither does rdantic, and to_json() therefore writes a JSON array. A property is required unless it declares a default, which is the same rule %default% follows for struct fields.

Vector <- new_class("Vector", properties = list(x = class_double))
from_list(Vector, list(x = c(1, 2, 3)))@x
#> [1] 1 2 3

Native S7’s new_class() does not accept rdantic expressions such as num[1] as property classes. To require exactly one double, define the S7 class through rdantic:

Scalar <- s7_struct("Scalar", x = num[1])
Scalar(x = 1)
#> <Scalar>
#>  @ x: num 1
Scalar(x = c(1, 2))
#> Error:
#> ! 1 validation problem in <Scalar>
#>   @x  expected num[1], got num[2]  -- length is 2, not 1

class_data.frame similarly says only that the value is a data frame; it says nothing about column names or types. rdantic preserves that meaning. Use an rdantic frame(id = int, name = chr) field when you want a particular table shape.

S7 details and boundaries

The conversion keeps S7’s own behavior around the translated fields:

  • A property with a getter but no setter is computed. It is omitted from parsing, schemas and serialization because callers cannot supply it. A property with both a getter and setter remains a field.
  • Constant and expression-valued S7 defaults make a property optional. Expressions are left for S7 to evaluate for each new object rather than being evaluated by rdantic.
  • The class’s S7 validator still runs when rdantic constructs an object. An abstract S7 class can describe and validate existing objects, but a list cannot be parsed into a new instance of it.
  • Unknown input keys are ignored when parsing into an existing S7 class. Classes made by s7_struct() can instead use .extra = "forbid".

An existing object of the requested class is returned unchanged. Use from_list() or from_json() on incoming data when parsing and path-aware validation at a boundary is the goal.

Declaring an S7 class with rdantic types

s7_struct() is struct() with an S7 class as the result. The fields are written exactly as they would be for a struct, and every property validates through its rdantic type – on construction and on @<-:

Account <- s7_struct("Account",
  id     = int[1][. > 0],
  email  = chr[1][grepl("@", ., fixed = TRUE)],
  credit = num[1][. >= 0] %default% 0
)

a <- Account(id = 1, email = "ada@example.org")
a@credit
#> [1] 0

Coercion happens exactly where rdantic would coerce it, so the property holds the value rdantic promised rather than the one you happened to type:

a@credit <- 10L
typeof(a@credit)
#> [1] "double"

and the failures are the same typed_errors, with the property named as @field:

a@id <- 0
#> Error:
#> ! 1 validation problem in <Account>
#>   @id  expected int[1][. > 0], got num[1] 0
Account(id = 1)
#> Error:
#> ! 1 validation problem in <Account>
#>   @email  expected chr[1][grepl("@", ., fixed = TRUE)], got <missing>

The result is an ordinary S7 class, so S7 generics dispatch on it:

balance <- new_generic("balance", "x")
method(balance, Account) <- function(x) x@credit
balance(a)
#> [1] 10

and an ordinary rdantic type, so it parses, validates and describes itself:

from_json(Account, '{"id": 2, "email": "bob@example.org"}')
#> <Account>
#>  @ id    : int 2
#>  @ email : chr "bob@example.org"
#>  @ credit: num 0
schema(Account)$properties$id
#> $type
#> [1] "integer"
#> 
#> $description
#> [1] "satisfies . > 0"

Properties are declared class_any, deliberately: the real constraint is the rdantic type, and a second, weaker check by S7 would only be able to disagree with it. The field types are kept on the class, which is why int[1][. > 0] survives above rather than decaying to anything.

One deliberate difference from struct(): the name is not registered, so ref() and opt("Account") will not find it. A name in that registry means something that builds instances, and this builds S7 objects. Pass the class itself instead – it is a value, and a type.

Inheritance

.parent takes an S7 class, whose properties are inherited as typed fields:

Premium <- s7_struct("Premium", tier = one_of("gold", "silver"), .parent = Account)

p <- Premium(id = 1, email = "ada@example.org", tier = "gold")
class(p)
#> [1] "Premium"   "Account"   "S7_object"
fields(Premium)
#> [1] "id"     "email"  "credit" "tier"

There is one case rdantic can express and S7 cannot. rdantic lets a child retype an inherited field; S7 keeps the parent’s property definition and silently ignores a redeclaration. Rather than hand back a class whose narrower type is never enforced, the hierarchy is flattened – the type is honoured, the S7_inherits() relationship is not – and you are told:

Big <- s7_struct("Big", id = int[1][. > 100], .parent = Account)
#> Warning: <Big> retypes `id`, which S7 cannot override on a parent class; the S7
#> class is flattened and does not inherit from <Account>
class(Big(id = 101, email = "ada@example.org"))
#> [1] "Big"       "S7_object"
Big(id = 1, email = "ada@example.org")
#> Error:
#> ! 1 validation problem in <Big>
#>   @id  expected int[1][. > 100], got num[1] 1

Converting an existing struct

When the struct already exists – because other code parses into it, or it is reached by ref() – as_s7_class() converts it rather than redeclaring it:

Animal <- struct("Animal", name = chr[1], legs = int[1])
Dog    <- extend(Animal, "Dog", good = lgl[1] %default% TRUE)

d <- as_s7_class(Dog)(name = "Rex", legs = 4L)
class(d)
#> [1] "Dog"       "Animal"    "S7_object"
S7_inherits(d, as_s7_class(Animal))
#> [1] TRUE

extend() becomes S7 inheritance, under the same flattening rule as above. Unlike s7_struct(), as_s7_class() caches by name and field signature, so converting the same struct twice returns the same class and S7_inherits() keeps working.

extend() and partial() also accept an S7 class directly, and read its properties as typed fields – so you can go back to plain lists at any point:

fields(extend(Account, "AccountNote", note = chr[1]))
#> [1] "id"     "email"  "credit" "note"
fields(partial(Account))
#> [1] "id"     "email"  "credit"

In short

Use an S7 class directly when it is already your domain model and rdantic belongs at the input boundary. Use s7_struct() when you are declaring the model with rdantic types but downstream code expects S7. Use as_s7_class() when the rdantic struct already exists and you need an S7 view of it.
